title: What Counts as Deviance
description: Norms and sanctions, why verdicts on the same act shift, and Durkheim's claim that crime is normal

concepts.title: Norms, Sanctions and the Meaning of Deviance
concepts.contentHtml:
Drink your soup straight from the bowl at a formal dinner and people stare. Take a stranger's wallet and you may end up in court. Sociologists put both under one heading: deviance, behaviour (or sometimes a belief or condition) that breaks the norms of a group, its shared expectations about how people ought to act. Crime is the narrower set of deviant acts that the state has written into law and punishes.

The American sociologist William Graham Sumner gave the field its first vocabulary in Folkways (1906). Folkways are everyday customs that grow up without anyone planning them, as people solve recurring problems: how to greet, what to wear, how to eat. When a group comes to see a custom as vital to its welfare, it becomes one of the mores, which carry moral weight, so breaking one provokes outrage rather than mild disapproval. Sumner was struck by how much power this gives a culture: "At every turn we find new evidence that the mores can make anything right." Laws are the formal layer on top, rules the state enforces through police and courts.

Every norm comes with sanctions, rewards for conformity and penalties for breaches. They can be informal (a raised eyebrow, gossip, losing friends) or formal (a fine, dismissal, a criminal record). Most of the order you live in is kept by informal sanctions; the formal ones are the last line of defence.

Two points keep the idea honest. First, calling an act deviant is a description, not a verdict: it records that a group treats the act as a breach, whatever the sociologist thinks of it. Campaigners for causes that later won, from religious toleration to votes for women, were deviant in their own day. Second, deviance and crime only partly overlap. Plenty of deviance is legal, such as turning up to a job interview in fancy dress, and some crime, such as nudging past the speed limit on an empty road, is barely seen as deviant at all. The rest of this topic asks who decides which breaches count, and with what effect.

concepts.title: Same Act, Different Verdict
concepts.contentHtml:
What counts as deviant changes across time and place, often faster than people expect. Until 1961 it was a crime in England and Wales to take your own life. The Suicide Act 1961 ended that in one line: "The rule of law whereby it is a crime for a person to commit suicide is hereby abrogated.1" The act itself had not changed; the verdict had.

Drugs show the same pattern in reverse. In the 1930s cannabis was used in small circles in the United States, among them jazz musicians. Harry Anslinger, commissioner of the federal Bureau of Narcotics, turned his attention to it and pushed a bill through Congress to place it under the same tight control as heroin and cocaine. President Franklin Roosevelt signed the bill on 2 August 1937.2 The drug soon came to account for more federal enforcement activity than any other. A habit of a few became a national crime because a campaign made it one.

Sociologists call this the relativity of deviance, and it is worth being exact about what it claims. It is an empirical observation: different societies, and the same society at different dates, classify different acts as wrong and punish them differently. It is not the philosophical thesis of relativism, that nothing is really wrong. You can hold that killing for gain is wrong everywhere and still study why one era punishes an act savagely and another shrugs at it.

Relativity points you towards the rule-makers. Someone drafts each statute, lobbies for it and decides where police attention goes. Conflict theorists, met in the modern theory topic, ask whose interests those choices serve. Lesson 3 shows how the very idea of crime was once narrowed to the offences of the poor, and Lesson 5 follows the campaigners Howard Becker called moral entrepreneurs, of whom Anslinger is a textbook example.

concepts.title: Durkheim: Why Crime Is Normal
concepts.contentHtml:
In The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) Émile Durkheim made a claim that still startles readers: crime is normal. He did not mean it is good. He meant it is universal: "Crime is not only observed in most societies of a particular species, but in all societies of all types.1" The acts called criminal change, but no society has ever been free of them. (Durkheim's wider sociology belongs to the classical theory topic; here you need only this argument.)

His reasoning runs like this. A crime offends collective feelings that are especially strong and clear. For crime to vanish, everyone would have to share those feelings with enough force to resist every temptation. But if feelings grew that strong, people would also become more sensitive to lesser faults, and some of those would be reclassified as crimes. His thought experiment: "Imagine a community of saints in an exemplary and perfect monastery.2" Crime as such would be unknown there, yet small lapses would cause the scandal that ordinary crimes cause elsewhere, and the community would punish them as crimes. You cannot abolish deviance; you can only move the line.

Deviance also does work for a society:

  • Boundary-setting: punishing a breach shows everyone where the line is and draws the law-abiding together in shared disapproval.
  • Change: today's offender can be tomorrow's pioneer. "According to Athenian law, Socrates was a criminal and his condemnation was entirely just," Durkheim wrote, yet Socrates's independence of thought helped prepare the new morality Athens needed.

Durkheim guarded against misreading in a footnote: "although crime is a fact of normal sociology, it does not follow that we should not abhor it." Pain is normal too, and useful, and nobody likes it. The idea that deviance is built into social life, rather than being a sickness of a few individuals, is the starting point for every theory in this topic.

title: Strain: When Goals Outrun Means
description: Merton's five adaptations, delinquent subcultures, and Agnew's general strain theory with the evidence

concepts.title: Merton: Goals, Means and Five Adaptations
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1938 Robert K. Merton published "Social Structure and Anomie" in the American Sociological Review, borrowing Durkheim's word for normlessness to explain why some societies produce more crime than others. (Merton's place in functionalism is covered in the modern theory topic; the focus here is deviance.) His key distinction was between cultural goals, what a society teaches everyone to want, and institutional means, the approved ways of getting it, such as education and steady work.

Trouble comes when the two fall out of balance. American culture held up money as the measure of success for everyone, while the class structure gave many people little real chance of earning it legitimately. Antisocial behaviour appears on a large scale, Merton wrote, "only when a system of cultural values extols, virtually above all else, certain common symbols of success for the population at large1 while its social structure rigorously restricts or completely eliminates access to approved modes of acquiring these symbols for a considerable part of the same population." He mapped the possible responses:

  • Conformity: accept both goals and means; the most common response.
  • Innovation: keep the goal, drop the approved means: fraud, theft, organised vice.
  • Ritualism: give up the goal as out of reach but keep following the rules to the letter.
  • Retreatism: abandon both goals and means and withdraw.
  • Rebellion: reject both and try to put new goals and means in their place.

The surprising part is what Merton said about poverty. Poverty alone, he argued, does not produce a high crime rate. It does so when combined with a culture that tells the poor they too should be rich. "Thus, poverty is less highly correlated with crime in southeastern Europe than in the United States,2" he wrote, because in a more rigid class order fewer people were taught to expect to rise.

concepts.title: Subcultures: Status Frustration and Unequal Opportunity
concepts.contentHtml:
Merton described individual adaptations, but delinquency usually happens in groups, with their own codes and loyalties. In the 1950s sociologists explained this with the delinquent subculture: a set of values a group builds when the mainstream route to respect is closed.

Albert Cohen, in Delinquent Boys (1955), started at school. Working-class boys were judged against a "middle-class measuring rod" that their upbringing had not prepared them to meet, and many were found lacking.1 The result was status frustration. Their collective solution was to flip the standards, making the opposite of middle-class respectability a source of prestige. Cohen called the resulting subculture "nonutilitarian, malicious, and negativistic". That phrase captured something Merton's theory missed: much youth crime, such as vandalism or fighting, brings in no money at all.

Richard Cloward and Lloyd Ohlin (Delinquency and Opportunity, 1960) added a twist. Illegitimate opportunities, like legitimate ones, are unequally spread, so the shape of a neighbourhood decides which subculture forms:

  • a criminal subculture, offering a career ladder in theft and rackets. It needs some coordination between the underworld and people in legitimate roles, such as politicians or police;2 think of the old political machine protecting favoured rackets.
  • a conflict subculture, built on violence, in the "disorganized slum" where legitimate and illegitimate worlds are not linked and nothing restrains street gangs.
  • a retreatist subculture of drug use, for "double failures" who succeed in neither world.

Both theories were built almost entirely on studies of boys. Later work, such as John Hagan's power-control theory, set out to explain the large and persistent gender gap in delinquency that the subcultural tradition took for granted.

concepts.title: General Strain and Institutional Anomie
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1970s strain theory had powerful critics, among them the control theorist Travis Hirschi (Lesson 4), and it fell out of favour. It returned in the late 1980s and 1990s in two new forms, one aimed at individuals and one at whole societies.1

Robert Agnew's general strain theory (1992) widened what counts as strain. He identified three major sources:

  • the failure to achieve positively valued goals, including the gap between what you expect, or think fair, and what you actually get;
  • the removal, or threatened removal, of something you value;
  • the presentation of negative or noxious stimuli, such as abuse.

Strain produces negative emotions such as anger, frustration, depression and anxiety, and crime is one way to relieve them: to get what you want, to hit back, or to escape. Whether strain becomes delinquency depends on coping resources, such as self-esteem, social support and problem-solving skills, and on whether your friends approve of offending. Many studies support the core prediction that greater exposure to strain goes with more offending.

Institutional anomie theory, developed by Steven Messner and Richard Rosenfeld from 1994, went back to Merton's level of the whole society. Its claim is that where the economy dominates the other institutions, family, school and politics bend to market values and lose their power to restrain. In their words, "economic dominance stimulates the emergence of anomie at the cultural level, and... erodes the structural restraints against crime associated with the performance of institutional roles." The theory has mostly been used to explain trends in crime rates across whole societies rather than individual choices.

Notice the shift. Merton's strain was about money and class; Agnew's is about any painful experience, which lets strain theory explain offending by the comfortable as well as the poor.

title: Learning Crime and Crimes of the Powerful
description: Sutherland's differential association, techniques of neutralisation, and the discovery of white-collar crime

concepts.title: Differential Association: Crime Is Learned
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early twentieth century many criminologists looked for the causes of crime inside individuals: in heredity, low intelligence or a disordered personality. Edwin Sutherland offered a flatly social alternative. Criminal behaviour, he argued, is learned like any other behaviour, through interaction with other people, above all in close personal groups.

His theory of differential association (1939, revised over the next decade) says that what you learn has two parts. There are techniques, such as how to pick a lock or falsify accounts. And there are definitions: the motives, attitudes and rationalisations that make breaking the law seem acceptable or unacceptable. Everyone hears both kinds. Delinquent behaviour is "learned in association with those who define such behavior favorably and in isolation from those who define it unfavorably,1" and it occurs when "the weight of the favorable definitions exceeds the weight of the unfavorable definitions."

Two features made the theory radical. It was general: Sutherland meant one mechanism to explain juvenile delinquency, professional theft and the crimes of businessmen alike. And the associations that mattered were of ideas as much as of people. The concept, as one review puts it, "referred not only to associations among people but also, and perhaps even more important, to associations among ideas." The executive who learns over lunch that price-fixing is simply how the industry works is learning in the same way as the apprentice burglar.

The theory's main weakness is the direction of cause. Teenagers with delinquent friends tend to offend more, but the link can run both ways: delinquents may also choose delinquent friends. Separating influence from selection remains one of the hardest problems in the study of peers, and later social learning theories grew out of attempts to solve it.

concepts.title: Techniques of Neutralisation
concepts.contentHtml:
If crime is learned, what exactly is learned? In 1957 Sykes and Matza pointed to something awkward for subcultural theories: delinquents who are caught usually show guilt or shame, just as white-collar offenders do.1 If they had truly adopted an inverted set of values, they should feel proud. Sykes and Matza concluded that most delinquents share conventional values and drift into offending through a subtle process of justification that switches off the moral brakes for a while.

"We call these justifications of deviant behavior techniques of neutralization," they wrote, "and we believe these techniques make up a crucial component of Sutherland's definitions favorable to the violation of law." The techniques include:

  • Denial of responsibility: "it wasn't my fault", blaming a bad upbringing, drink or bad company.
  • Denial of injury: "nobody really got hurt"; the shop is insured anyway.
  • Condemnation of the condemners: the police and teachers are hypocrites or biased, so who are they to judge?
  • Appeal to higher loyalties: "I did it for my mates", or for the family or the gang.

The idea reaches well beyond teenagers. Sutherland had argued that people become white-collar criminals because they are immersed with their colleagues in a business ideology that defines illegal practices as acceptable. Neutralisations are the everyday vocabulary of that ideology: "everyone in the industry does it", "the regulations are absurd", "no real person lost out". Notice what the techniques do. They are learned, as Sutherland said, but their effect is to loosen a person's tie to rules they still believe in. That makes neutralisation a bridge between learning theories and the control theories of the next lesson.

concepts.title: White-Collar Crime: Sutherland's Provocation
concepts.contentHtml:
In his 1939 presidential address to the American Sociological Society, Sutherland used a phrase that stuck: white-collar crime, crime committed by people of respectability and high social status in the course of their occupations. His target was criminology itself. When he spoke, crime was seen as something that happened mainly among immigrants and poor people,1 and theories built on poverty or broken homes could say nothing about a respectable banker's fraud.

His book White Collar Crime (1949) studied seventy of the two hundred largest US non-financial corporations. Counting decisions by courts and regulators against them for offences such as antitrust violations and false advertising, he found 980 adverse decisions against the seventy, an average of 14 each:2 a record that, in an individual, would mark a persistent offender.

Critics objected at once. Tappan argued in 1947 that white-collar offences are not "crimes" if they fall outside legal definitions, and many of Sutherland's decisions were civil or administrative, not criminal convictions. Sutherland's defenders reply that the choice to handle such conduct through regulators rather than prosecutors is itself shaped by the offenders' power. That is the social-construction argument of Lesson 1 in its sharpest form: the boundary of "crime" is drawn by people, and some people have more say in where it goes.

The scale is hard to measure but large. Reiman, updating US Chamber of Commerce estimates, put the 1991 cost of white-collar offences such as consumer fraud, embezzlement and securities fraud at $197.76 billion. He noted that this was "almost 6000 times the total amount taken in all bank-robberies in the US in 19913". Yet such offences barely register in the crime counts of Lesson 6: the Office for National Statistics warns that recorded fraud is not a reliable measure because so many incidents are never reported.

title: Why Don't We All Offend? Control and the Life Course
description: Hirschi's social bond, self-control and the age-crime curve, and Laub and Sampson's turning points

concepts.title: Hirschi's Question: Why Do Most People Conform?
concepts.contentHtml:
Strain and learning theories ask why people break rules. Travis Hirschi turned the question round. In Causes of Delinquency (1969) he treated the temptation to cheat, steal or fight as ordinary, needing no special explanation. What needs explaining is conformity. His answer: people conform when their bond to society is strong and deviate when it is weak or broken. As one review puts it, "no special strain between goals and means is necessarily required to produce delinquent behavior; all that is required is the elimination of the constraining elements of the social bond.1"

The bond has four elements:

  • Attachment: caring about the opinions of parents, teachers and friends, so that their disapproval hurts.
  • Commitment: investment in conventional goals, such as exams, a job or a reputation, that offending would put at risk.
  • Involvement: time taken up by conventional activities, leaving less for trouble.
  • Belief: accepting that the rules are legitimate and ought to be obeyed.

Hirschi tested the theory on a sample of 4,077 students from 11 junior and senior high schools in the Richmond, California, area in 1964,2 asking about both their bonds and the offences they had committed; most of his tests used only the white boys in the sample. Stronger attachment, commitment and belief went with less delinquency, a pattern later research has largely confirmed. Involvement was the surprise. Time spent on sports, hobbies, television or paid work was not associated with delinquency,3 which Hirschi explained by pointing out that most delinquent acts take very little time.

Control has a neighbourhood version too. From the late 1920s Clifford Shaw and Henry McKay mapped delinquency across Chicago4 and found it concentrated where poverty, residential turnover and ethnic mixing were high. They read these as signs of social disorganisation: neighbourhoods whose bonds and controls had weakened, so that they could not realise the goals of their own residents. Lesson 7 meets the idea again in its modern form, collective efficacy.

concepts.title: Self-Control and the Age-Crime Curve
concepts.contentHtml:
One fact about crime is so regular that every theory must face it: offending rises through the teenage years and falls away in adulthood. Most delinquents "age out" of delinquency. Yet, as the criminologist John Hagan observed, "our theories are much more attentive to why young people become delinquent than to why they stop being so." The decline matters for policy. A 2014 review by the US National Research Council concluded that "because offending declines markedly with age, the incapacitation effect of very long sentences is likely to be small.1"

In A General Theory of Crime (1990) Michael Gottfredson and Travis Hirschi moved control theory inside the person. Their explanation rests on a single trait, low self-control: being impulsive, short-sighted and drawn to risk. Crime offers quick, easy rewards, so people low in self-control commit more of it when opportunity arises. In their account the propensity is formed early, largely through how children are raised, and then stays fairly stable; what changes over the life course is opportunity.

The theory is popular partly because it travels. Low self-control predicts self-reported offending across many groups, including, for example, a study of 382 American Indian teenagers. And it suggests why environmental damage to the developing brain, such as childhood lead exposure (Lesson 6), might raise crime: lead is associated with greater impulsivity.

Its critics ask the obvious question. If self-control is stable, why do almost all offenders slow down, and why do some stop abruptly? A stable trait cannot by itself explain a change. Life-course criminologists answered that what happens in adulthood can redirect a life, and they had the data to show it.

concepts.title: Turning Points: Laub and Sampson
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1986 John Laub found boxes of old research files in the basement of Harvard Law School.1 They held the data of Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck, who had studied 500 boys sent to reform school in the 1930s, collecting information about each of them at ages 14, 25 and 32. With Robert Sampson, Laub computerised the records and then traced the men again in their late 60s, combining new interviews with official records. The results appeared in Crime in the Making (1993) and Shared Beginnings, Divergent Lives: Delinquent Boys to Age 70 (2003), together the longest life-course study of criminal behaviour ever conducted.

The boys had looked like textbook future criminals, yet their adult lives diverged widely. Laub and Sampson found that even highly active offenders could stop after key turning points: marriage, military service, steady employment, and joining institutions and social networks that cut them off from offending peers. They concluded that "desistance from crime is a process, not an event2". In control terms, a turning point builds new bonds, new routines and people who care, and gives a man something to lose.

This joins the control tradition to the life course. Hirschi's bonds are not fixed in adolescence: they can be rebuilt decades later, and a bond acquired at 30 can pull someone away from crime. It also links back to strain and labelling. A record that shuts someone out of steady work, as Lesson 5 shows, removes one of the strongest routes out of crime.

The study carries a methodological lesson too. "Lives are lived forward but can only be understood backwards," as Laub put it, which is why only long panel studies, following the same people for decades, can show how criminal careers end. Laub and Sampson shared the Stockholm Prize in Criminology in 2011.

title: Labelling, Stigma and Moral Panics
description: How reactions create deviant careers, what a criminal record costs, and what the experiments show

concepts.title: Labelling: Deviance as a Reaction
concepts.contentHtml:
Every theory so far asks why people break rules. Labelling theory asks what happens when others react. In 1938 Frank Tannenbaum argued that a young person's first contact with the law can be decisive,1 a "dramatization of evil" that singles the child out and shifts attention from the act to the person. "The way out," he wrote, "is through a refusal to dramatize the evil."

Edwin Lemert named the two stages. Primary deviance is the initial rule-breaking, often casual or random, with little effect on how you see yourself. Secondary deviance follows the social reaction: treated as a delinquent, a thief or an addict, a person may reorganise their identity and life around the label. Howard Becker gave the radical version in Outsiders (1963): deviance "is not a quality of the act the person commits, but rather a consequence of the application by others of rules and sanctions to an 'offender'." A later critic, Johannes Knutsson, summed up the position in one line: "Deviant behavior is behavior which is so labeled.2"

Becker drew a simple grid. Cross whether someone broke a rule with whether they are seen as deviant, and you get four types:

  • Conforming: obeys the rule and is not labelled.
  • Pure deviant: breaks the rule and is labelled.
  • Secret deviant: breaks the rule unnoticed.
  • Falsely accused: is labelled without having broken it.

Official statistics see only the labelled cells, which is one reason labelling theorists distrusted them. Becker also turned attention to the rule-makers, the moral entrepreneurs: individuals who develop a strong stake in moral crusading and devote unusual time and energy to it. Harry Anslinger, whose 1937 campaign against cannabis you met in Lesson 1, fits the description exactly. Every new rule, on this view, creates a new class of outsiders.

concepts.title: Stigma and the Mark of a Criminal Record
concepts.contentHtml:
Erving Goffman's Stigma (1963) took labelling into everyday encounters. A stigma, he wrote, is "an attribute which is deeply discrediting1", but he added that "a language of relationships, not attributes, is really needed": a mark spoils an identity only in the eyes of an audience. (Goffman's wider sociology is covered in the modern theory topic.) He separated the discredited, whose stigma is known or visible, from the discreditable, whose stigma is hidden and must be managed: whom to tell, when and how much. A criminal record is a classic discreditable mark, invisible until a form asks the question.

What does that mark cost? Between June and December 2001 the sociologist Devah Pager ran an audit experiment in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Pairs of young men, matched on age, race, appearance and qualifications, applied in person for real entry-level jobs at 350 employers. In each pair one man presented himself as recently released from prison after a felony drug conviction. The callback rates:

  • White applicants: 34 per cent without a record, 17 per cent with one.
  • Black applicants: 14 per cent without a record, 5 per cent with one.

A record halved a white applicant's chances.2 And a white man fresh out of prison did about as well as a Black man with no record at all, a finding about race as striking as the one about records. Two details sharpen the picture: about three-quarters of the employers asked about convictions, yet only 4 of the 350 checked references.3 They were screening on the label, not the person.

Pager drew the labelling conclusion herself. Steady work is one of the strongest predictors of leaving crime, so "we may be exacerbating the very conditions that lead to crime in the first place." Stigma can help produce the reoffending it claims to predict.

concepts.title: Testing Labelling: Experiments, Critics and Panics
concepts.contentHtml:
Labelling theory makes a testable prediction: formally processing young offenders should, on average, make them offend more, not less. Between 1973 and 2008 researchers published 29 randomised experiments that assigned young people either to the juvenile justice system or to diversion (release, or a programme instead of court). In 2010 Anthony Petrosino, Carolyn Turpin-Petrosino and Sarah Guckenburg pooled them for the Campbell Collaboration: 7,304 juveniles in all. Processing had no crime-control effect.1 Across measures of prevalence, incidence, severity and self-report, it appeared to increase delinquency.

That is strong support, but the authors note that labelling is not the only explanation: court processing might also do harm by exposing young people to more delinquent peers. The theory has older critics too. In 1977 Knutsson, writing for Sweden's National Council for Crime Prevention, argued that saying groups "create" deviance by making rules comes close to a truism; that labelling theorists showed little interest in the causes of primary deviance; and that defining deviance purely by reaction deprives an individual's actions of moral and social meaning.2 Becker's secret deviant is a puzzle on his own terms: if nobody reacted, in what sense is the act deviant?

Labelling can also work on a whole society. Stanley Cohen's Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972), which you may know from the Monster Panics topic, studied the alarm over clashes between Mods and Rockers at English seaside towns in the 1960s. Cohen argued that the reaction of press, police and politicians amplified the very behaviour it condemned. Stuart Hall and colleagues' Policing the Crisis (1978), covered in Media Theory, traced a similar spiral around "mugging" in 1970s Britain. A moral panic is labelling at the scale of a nation, and its test is the same: does the reaction fit the harm?

title: Counting Crime and the Great Crime Drop
description: Police records against victim surveys, the drop nobody predicted, and the lead and abortion hypotheses

concepts.title: The Dark Figure: Two Ways to Count
concepts.contentHtml:
How much crime is there? The answer depends on the instrument, and the two main instruments disagree. Police recorded crime counts offences reported to and recorded by the police. It misses everything victims never report, the dark figure of crime, and it shifts whenever reporting habits or recording rules change. The dark figure is large: in the United States, the Bureau of Justice Statistics found that in 2022 only 41.5 per cent of violent crimes and 31.8 per cent of household property crimes were reported to the police.1

Victimisation surveys go round the police by asking a random sample of people what has happened to them. America's National Crime Victimization Survey began in 1973. The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW), originally the British Crime Survey, was first run in 1982, covering crime in 1981; its estimates for the year to March 2026 rest on face-to-face interviews with 31,350 adults. Surveys capture unreported crime but have blind spots of their own. The CSEW does not cover crimes against businesses or people living outside private households, it cannot interview murder victims, and it relies on people remembering and disclosing.

The two sources can tell different stories, because changes in police recording practices, especially for violence, move the recorded figures independently of crime itself. In 2014 the statistics regulator found that police recorded crime data might not be reliable and removed their accredited official statistics status.2 The Office for National Statistics now describes police figures as better indicators of police activity than crime trends, while preferring them for rare, serious offences such as homicide and offences involving weapons.

A third instrument, the self-report survey, asks people which offences they have committed; Hirschi's study in Lesson 4 used one. Labelling theorists started from the assumption that nearly everyone breaks rules at some point, and self-reports were their natural tool for showing that official statistics reflect who gets caught as well as who offends. The working rule is triangulation: trust a trend when independent instruments agree.

concepts.title: The Drop Nobody Predicted
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1990s many experts expected a wave of youth violence. Instead, US crime fell fast. Homicide rates fell 43 per cent from their 1991 peak to 2001, wrote the economist Steven Levitt, and the decline came "essentially without warning: leading experts were predicting an explosion in crime in the early and mid-1990s, precisely the point when crime rates began to plunge.1"

The fall kept going. Using FBI data, Pew Research Center calculated that the US violent crime rate fell 49 per cent between 1993 and 2022; on the victimisation survey, violent and property crime each fell 71 per cent. In England and Wales, the CSEW put violence in the year to June 2026 at 79 per cent below its 1995 peak,2 and theft 77 per cent below. Across North America, Europe and Australasia, many common crimes fell by half or more from the early 1990s. Fraud and online crime are the big exceptions.

Here is the surprise: the public mostly did not notice. In 23 of 27 Gallup surveys since 1993, at least 60 per cent of US adults said there was more crime nationally than a year before,3 even while the rate fell. Far fewer said crime was rising in their own area.

The international reach of the drop is itself evidence. Graham Farrell, Nick Tilley and Andromachi Tseloni tested 17 proposed explanations against facts any answer must fit, such as the drop occurring in many countries at once while some crimes rose. Sixteen failed at least one test. The one that passed was the security hypothesis: better locks, alarms and above all electronic immobilisers made cars far harder to steal. Cars with central locking plus an immobiliser were up to 25 times less likely to be stolen than unprotected ones,4 and UK car theft fell by two-thirds from the mid-1990s. Because property crimes are often the first offences in a criminal career, fewer easy opportunities may also have meant fewer careers.

concepts.title: Lead, Abortion and Levitt's Scorecard
concepts.contentHtml:
The US drop prompted two of the boldest hypotheses in social science. Both rely on a delay: something changed in the 1970s that lowered offending about twenty years later, when the children affected reached the peak ages for crime.

  • Abortion. John Donohue and Steven Levitt argued in 2001 that legalising abortion in the early 1970s played an important role in the 1990s drop, on two premises: unwanted children are at greater risk of crime, and legal abortion reduces unwanted births. In 2019, with 17 more years of data, they estimated that legal abortion cut crime by roughly 20 per cent between 1997 and 2014.1 Christopher Foote and Christopher Goetz found a coding mistake in one of the original analyses and showed that fixing it and measuring crime per head generates much weaker results.2 Donohue and Levitt accepted the error but argued that better measures of abortion exposure restore their findings.3 The dispute is not settled.
  • Lead. Childhood lead exposure is linked to aggressive and criminal behaviour. Lead was removed from US petrol under the Clean Air Act from the late 1970s, and Jessica Wolpaw Reyes (2007) used the uneven state-by-state timing to credit it with significant declines in 1990s violent crime. A 2022 meta-analysis of 542 estimates from 24 studies found the effect real but overstated by publication bias: lead's removal may explain 7 to 28 per cent of the US fall in homicide, but not most of the drop.4

Levitt's own 2004 scorecard credited four factors: the increasing number of police, the skyrocketing number of prisoners, the ebbing of the crack epidemic5 and legalised abortion. He rejected six popular ones, including the strong economy, changing demographics and better policing strategies. Note the method. Every claim here rests on natural experiments, comparing places that changed at different times, the tools of The Credibility Revolution topic. The next lesson takes on the two most politically charged items: police and prisons.

title: Policing and Punishment: What the Evidence Shows
description: Broken windows on trial, whether more police cut crime, and what mass imprisonment bought

concepts.title: Broken Windows on Trial
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1982, in an article in the Atlantic Monthly, James Q. Wilson and George Kelling argued that minor disorder, such as an unrepaired window, graffiti or public drinking, signals that nobody is in control and invites more serious crime. Police should therefore target disorder itself. More than twenty years later, New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, the three most populous US cities, had all adopted some version of the idea.

The evidence has been fought over ever since:

  • For: Kelling and William Sousa (2001) found that New York precincts with more arrests for minor offences saw bigger falls in serious crime, and Corman and Mocan reached a similar conclusion from city-wide trends.
  • Against: Bernard Harcourt and Jens Ludwig (2006) showed that the precinct pattern fits mean reversion: the precincts policed hardest in the 1990s were those where crime had risen most in the crack epidemic, and such places tend to fall back furthest anyway. In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, about 4,600 low-income families were randomly given vouchers to move to less disorderly neighbourhoods; the authors found no support for a simple disorder-crime link.1
  • Common causes: Robert Sampson and Stephen Raudenbush had observers videotape more than 23,000 streets in 196 Chicago neighbourhoods. Disorder and crime both stemmed from concentrated poverty, and both were lower where collective efficacy, neighbours' cohesion and willingness to act, was strong. Disorder was directly linked only to robbery.2

Meta-analysis gives the clearest summary. Anthony Braga, Brandon Welsh and Cory Schnell (2015) pooled 30 rigorous tests and found a modest overall crime reduction from disorder policing. But the type mattered. Community and problem-solving work to change disorderly places showed the strongest effects, while aggressive order maintenance, cracking down on individual minor offenders, did not produce significant crime reductions.3 Their 2024 update, with 59 tests, found the same split. "Broken windows" can mean fixing a place or arresting its people, and the evidence favours the first.

concepts.title: Do More Police Cut Crime?
concepts.contentHtml:
The question sounds simple, but a naive comparison misleads. Cities with more crime hire more police, so police and crime rise together even if police prevent crime: the reverse-causality problem from the Econometrics topic. You need a change in policing that has nothing to do with local crime.

London supplied one. After the terrorist bombings of 7 July 2005, police deployment in central London rose by over 30 per cent for six weeks,1 compared with outer London. Mirko Draca, Steve Machin and Robert Witt found that crime fell significantly in central relative to outer London during that time, and estimated that a 10 per cent increase in police activity reduces crime by around 3 per cent, an elasticity of about −0.3. Using data on US cities from 1960 to 2010, Aaron Chalfin and Justin McCrary argued that earlier studies were biased by mismeasured police numbers. Correcting for it, they estimated an elasticity of about −0.5, with police reducing violent crime more than property crime.

How police are used matters as much as how many there are. The National Institute of Justice, summarising Daniel Nagin's review of deterrence research, concludes that police deter crime by raising the perceived certainty of being caught.2 Strategies that use police as "sentinels", such as concentrating patrols on hot spots, the small places where crime clusters, are particularly effective. That fits Levitt's scorecard, which credited more police but not new policing strategies in general.

The live dispute is therefore less about whether police can reduce crime than about which tactics, and at what cost. Aggressive order maintenance has raised concerns about racial disparities in arrests, and the disorder-policing reviews found it bought no measurable crime reduction. Visible, targeted presence and problem-solving have the strongest evidence. Both sides of the policing debate now argue from the same body of causal studies, which is itself a kind of progress.

concepts.title: Prisons: What Mass Incarceration Bought
concepts.contentHtml:
After decades of stability from the 1920s to the early 1970s, the US incarceration rate more than quadrupled. State and federal prisoners rose from about 200,000 in 1973 to 1.5 million in 2009, and with local jails the US penal population reached 2.2 million adults, the largest in the world. In 2012 close to 25 per cent of the world's prisoners were held in American prisons, though the US has about 5 per cent of the world's people. The World Prison Brief's latest figures give about 542 prisoners per 100,000 people in the United States, against 140 in England and Wales, 54 in Norway and 33 in Japan.

Did it work? Prison can cut crime by incapacitation, since people inside cannot offend outside, and by deterrence, since the threat discourages others. Levitt credited the prison boom with a real share of the 1990s drop. The National Research Council's 2014 review was more cautious: the increase in incarceration may have caused a decrease in crime, but the size of the reduction is highly uncertain1 and most studies suggest it was unlikely to have been large. Two reasons stand out. Offending falls with age, so long sentences often hold people through years when they would have stopped anyway. And deterrence works mainly through certainty: the certainty of being caught is a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment,2 while raising severity does little.

Prison may even add to crime. Inmates can learn better techniques from each other, and the record they leave with carries the stigma Pager measured. The costs spread further. From 1980 to 2000 the number of American children with an imprisoned father rose from about 350,000 to 2.1 million,3 and incarceration has become another strand in the disadvantage of the poorest communities, though how much it worsens their conditions remains uncertain.

Here the topic's threads meet: Durkheim's punishment as boundary-setting, labelling's secondary deviance, and the careful causal estimates of modern criminology.
